catalog_quote: (16) Syllabic Maximality (SYL ≤ µµ): Banawá syllables are maximally bimoraic. ... As originally described in BBE, Banawá stresses every other mora from left-to-right within the word, skipping word-initial vowels in words with more than two syllables. The words in (46) illustrate the basic stress rule: (46) a. súirì 'penis' b. wárabù 'ear' c. wánakàri 'spider' d. yífuyà 'fire' e. uwárià 'one' f. úwi 'cry' ... its basic stress pattern is indeed a common left-to-right moraic trochaic system. ... (47) Foot Binarity (FTBIN): Feet are binary (on moras). (48) ALIGN FT: (FT, L, PRWD, L) ... Feet are bimoraic in Banawá with the exception of word-final, monomoraic feet in words of odd-numbered moras (omitting word-initial vowels). ... (69) ... e. máka rì 'cloth' ... its degenerate feet are neither restricted to "strong position", i.e. to where primary stress falls (see (69) above), nor are they completely unrestricted ... (83) a. kèrewéduàma 'turn end over end' b. (ke re) (wedu)(a ma) ... (84) a. tìkadámuèi 'you forget' b. (ti ka)(da mu)(uei) ... whereas Banawá diphthongs are all bimoraic, Suruwahá has only light, monomoraic diphthongs ... Suruwahá thus has syllabic iambs, whereas Banawá has moraic trochees. Interestingly, it is Suruwahá's iambic system which has lost the distinction between light and heavy syllables. This distinction has been maintained in the moraic, trochaic systems in Banawá. ... a result of the fact that SYLLINT is violated in Banawá foot construction
sweep_summary: Two title-hits for jama1261 (Madi; both actually about the Banawá variety, bana1307). (1) Buller, Buller & Everett 1993 (IJAL 59(3):280-293, DOI 10.1086/466199): open author copy on daneverettbooks. it is the original first-hand description that the catalog's current deciding source (Everett 1996 ROA-121) restates, and it confirms the weight coding (CV/CVV only, one mora per vowel, stress every other vowel L->R within the word, initial vowel extraprosodic except in bimoraic words, tautosyllabic vowels may belong to different feet) while adding, in n. 5, the hedged primary-stress rule (penultimate stress-bearing vowel, 'numerous exceptions') that Everett 1996 lacks in prose; recommended as the citation of record, with Everett 1996 kept for the degenerate-foot and diphthong-weight detail. (2) Wiltshire 2004, MA thesis (University of Manchester, 71 pp.) on stress in connected speech in Banawá: no online copy found (Glottolog record has no URL; Manchester Library Search returns 0 local hits for it; medium acquisition priority (first-hand, but phrase-level, and unlikely to displace BBE 1993). for the session was exhausted; all look-ups were done with direct download/automated download. Saved files and are under Manchester Library Search also surfaced two theoretical reanalyses of the BBE data not in the item list (Hyde, 'Issues in Banawá Prosody', LI; Martínez-Paricio & Kager, LI note on Banawá grid vs. metrical structure), not downloaded.

new_statements.quote: The basic statement of stress placement is easy: (skipping extraprosodic material), stress every other vowel (i.e., segments dominated by N) from left to right. [...] In words like those in (28)-(32), tautosyllabic vowels may belong to different metrical feet [...] [n. 5:] We have not yet completely analyzed the distinction between primary and secondary stress and so do not include a discussion of it in the text. However, it is generally the case that the penultimate secondary stress-bearing vowel receives primary stress.

new_statements.reading: Banawá (Madi) has iterative left-to-right binary left-headed (trochaic) feet built over vowels/moras within the grammatical word: every odd-numbered nucleus from the left is stressed, a word-initial vowel is extraprosodic (unstressed) in words of more than two vowels but stressed in bimoraic words (minimality), syllables are CV or CVV with one mora per vowel and feet may split a CVV syllable. Primary stress is only tentatively assigned (footnote): generally the penultimate stress-bearing vowel, with many exceptions. This is the peer-reviewed, first-hand description by the resident fieldworkers (the Bullers, ~six years with the Banawá; 1989 SIL corpus) that Everett 1996 restates; it confirms the catalog's 'weight' coding (CVV = two moras, mora-counting trochees) and supplies the primary-stress statement the current deciding source lacks in prose.

tone.quote: The overall pitch contour in Banawá shows very little variation in profiles. Syllables, whether accented or not, usually have falling pitch or in some rare cases stay level or rise. Accented syllables with pitch prominence are always high, never low, which allows us to predict the following two pitch movements: one with a jump up to the accented syllable and one with a jump down from the accented syllable. [...] Pitch accent in Banawá is used to indicate focus relations and contrast in combination with certain morphosyntactic means.

tone.summary: No lexical tone described: pitch functions intonationally (high pitch accents on stressed syllables marking focus/contrast, falling 'profile 1' vs rising 'profile 2'), on top of predictable trochaic word stress counted from the left edge.
